What Beijing Calls Open, Washington Should Call an Operation
item.description:
China is about to run the largest influence operation in history. It will not have to run it. The world will download it.

EXPERT PERSPECTIVE -- Our research team at Vanderbilt spent months inside the internal documents of GoLaxy, a Beijing firm - with ties to the Chinese state - that built a machine for shaping opinion abroad. Using AI, it generates personas, amplifies narratives that are favorable to Beijing and buries narratives that are not. And it’s been busy. It was used in Hong Kong to combat dissent against the National Security Law. It was used in Taiwan to sway the island’s 2024 [HWR1] elections.

Now consider what happens when it does not need to be built at all. If Chinese open-weight models — the ones that anyone can download, modify and run on their own machines — become the foundation that the world builds on, then the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) framing of Taiwan, Tiananmen, Xinjiang and Beijing itself ships inside every product that sits on top. No personas. No campaign. Just the default answer, everywhere. Something like this would make GoLaxy look like a dress rehearsal.

And here is the part that should stop Washington cold. Chinese models are about to be everywhere, and American strategy could allow it to happen. Washington is deciding whether to let frontier development run while clamping down on powerful open-weight models (whose safeguards can be stripped away). Here’s the deal though: restrictions would not kill demand for a cheap model that a company can download and make its own. China is standing at the counter with exactly that.

Today, we talk about the AI race as if it has one finish line. But it has two. The first is for frontier capability: who builds the most advanced models. American companies lead the way today. The second finish line is for reach: whose models become the foundation on which thousands of products are built? Chinese firms may have the advantage on this one. The first brings concentrated scientific, economic and military power. The second decides whose systems become the workhorses of ordinary life, and that reach shapes what people know and will learn in the future.

American frontier models like Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are closed, meaning you use them on the company's servers, and the company can cut off access. Chinese developers compete by releasing cheap open-weight models that companies can run on their own, with no provider to answer to. The babysitter has left the building.

This has already started. Airbnb relies on Alibaba's Qwen in its customer-service agent. Qwen, even briefly, powered a tool for searching proposed regulations on the Federal Register website. Amazon says thousands of customers have deployed DeepSeek through its cloud. In every case the interface is American. But the model underneath it is not.

Here’s something else to consider: Chinese developers must operate under Communist Party rules about what may be said. Those rules then shape which questions the models answer, which facts they omit and how they frame sensitive subjects. Open weights can be retuned, but scrubbing built-in defaults is expensive, and most companies will focus their efforts on addressing what matters to their business rather than check how a model handles every political subject. If a cheap Chinese model sits under thousands of products, its habits travel with it — into research tools, classroom software and fact-checkers — and the person on the other end never knows.

Beijing already knows about this risk. When Meta released its open-weight Llama models, Chinese regulators worried that a foreign model could "poison" China's AI ecosystem with information that the CCP censors. It seems to make sense that Washington should take seriously a vulnerability that Beijing recognized first.

None of this makes the open-weight safety problem smaller. In fact, just the opposite. Once a powerful open-weight model is released, its developer cannot recall it. Its safeguards can be stripped away and the model can be used for cyberattacks, the creation of biological weapons or worse. If we’re going to address this as a society, then testing requirements, liability rules and release restrictions are needed. But a Chinese open-weight model carries the same dangerous capabilities as an American one, and no American rule touches it.

If we constrain American developers and leave foreign weights untouched, demand will certainly shifts toward Chinese models. Theoretically, Washington could end up regulating the companies it can see while deepening its own dependence on the ones it cannot.

One answer might be to ban the Chinese models. But that means telling Americans which information technology they may use — and here lies the irony: the openness that protects Americans from domestic censorship may leave them exposed to systems built under Chinese censorship.

TikTok offers a glimpse of the stakes. More than 170 million Americans use it, and tens of millions say they get their news there. Washington spent five years fighting over its recommendation algorithm, and the deal that kept it in the United States required a change to that algorithm. But an algorithm only ranks videos that people make. While that fight dragged on, AI models learned to make the videos themselves — realistic footage with synced audio, from a sentence, in seconds. Three months after the deal closed, TikTok upgraded its ad tools to ByteDance’s newest video model. No rule required anyone to ask whose model was making the videos.

Now, you can see why the United States is facing a trilemma. It wants to prevent the uncontrolled release of dangerous AI capabilities. It wants to preserve Americans' freedom to choose their technology and information. And it wants to avoid dependence on models that are shaped inside an authoritarian system. It cannot fully secure all three.

Honest regulation starts by admitting that. Before restricting an U.S. model, ask which model developers will pick first. Domestic and foreign models distributed in the United States should face the same tests and the same rules. And companies that build products on a foundation model should have to say whose model it is.

AI leadership combines two things: the capability of a country's best models, and the reach of the models embedded in ordinary life. AI risk also combines two things: what a powerful model might do, and what a ubiquitous one tells people is true. GoLaxy showed us what Beijing can do with a machine to shape a belief. Now, what are we going to do about it?

item.title: Marine Le Pen as a Potential Instrument for Blocking European Support for Ukraine: The EU Budget, French Elections, and the Kremlin’s Strategic Interests
item.description:
Statements by Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (Rassemblement National, RN), threatening to block the European Union’s 2028–2034 budget and end bilateral military assistance to Ukraine suggest an intention to use a potential change of government in France to reshape European policy toward Russia. Her position goes beyond traditional Euroskepticism and could threaten Ukraine’s financial stability, EU unity, and European countries’ ability to sustain a long-term strategy of containing Moscow. The timing of these statements is particularly significant. The European Commission has already presented its proposal for the EU’s 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), totaling approximately €2 trillion, including a dedicated mechanism providing up to €100 billion in support for Ukraine. Budget negotiations are taking place amid rising defense expenditures, economic disagreements among member states, and uncertainty over the future direction of U.S. policy toward European security. The strategic danger is that electoral victories by political forces opposed to supporting Ukraine in key EU member states could turn budget negotiations into a mechanism for systematically weakening Europe’s policy of containing Russia. Why Le Pen’s Threat Carries Strategic Significance France is one of the European Union’s two nuclear powers, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, and a central player in shaping European defense policy. The potential rise to power of a political leadership opposed to extensive military assistance to Ukraine would therefore have consequences extending far beyond French-Ukrainian relations. Unlike Hungary or Slovakia, which have already used EU mechanisms to block or delay certain decisions concerning Ukraine, France carries considerably greater political weight. Its position could not only complicate decision-making but also alter the balance of power within the Union. Under Article 312 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Multiannual Financial Framework must be adopted unanimously by the Council of the EU after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament. A French government opposed to the proposed budget would therefore possess the legal means to block its approval. At the same time, the French president does not personally vote on the financial framework in the Council of the EU. Whether such a scenario could materialize would depend on the composition of the French government, the parliamentary majority, and the possibility of cohabitation between a president and prime minister from opposing political camps. The principal risk lies not only in a formal veto but also in the possibility of using the threat of a budget blockade to pressure other EU member states into reducing assistance to Ukraine. The EU Budget as an Instrument of Political Pressure The intention to block the 2028–2034 financial framework could serve several interconnected objectives. First, it creates an opportunity to undermine long-term financing for Ukraine. Unlike one-off assistance packages, multiyear budget mechanisms provide predictable funding for essential government functions, infrastructure reconstruction, and the country’s economic resilience. Second, blocking the budget could provoke a confrontation between countries determined to maintain support for Kyiv and those seeking to reduce their collective financial commitments. Third, a budget crisis could weaken the EU’s ability to finance its own defense industry, technological programs, and instruments of strategic autonomy. Such developments would benefit Moscow by allowing it to achieve some of its strategic objectives without entering into a direct military confrontation with NATO. Nevertheless, blocking the new financial framework would not automatically terminate all EU spending or assistance to Ukraine. EU treaties provide for the temporary continuation of existing budgetary ceilings and provisions, while member states could pursue alternative financing arrangements. Such solutions, however, could prove more expensive, politically complicated, and less predictable. Ending Military Assistance as a Factor Weakening European Deterrence Le Pen’s promise to terminate bilateral military assistance to Ukraine while preserving only basic training for Ukrainian military personnel carries not only material consequences but also significant political implications. France plays an important role in supplying weapons to Ukraine, developing defense cooperation, and shaping Europe’s collective response to Russian aggression. A French withdrawal from such support could produce three major consequences: The third consequence is potentially the most dangerous. If Moscow concludes that it merely needs to continue fighting until political leadership changes in major European countries, its incentive to engage in meaningful peace negotiations could diminish. Under such circumstances, European elections would become an integral element of Russia’s strategic calculations regarding the duration of its war against Ukraine. Le Pen’s Political Position and the Kremlin’s Interests Marine Le Pen’s long history of political contacts with Russia, her previous favorable statements about Vladimir Putin, and her party’s receipt of a loan from a Russian bank provide grounds for particular scrutiny of Moscow’s potential influence over the National Rally’s political agenda. In 2014, the then-National Front received a loan of approximately €9.4 million from Russia’s First Czech-Russian Bank. The transaction became a significant element of the debate surrounding financial ties between the French far right and Russia. However, it is essential to distinguish established facts, political affinity, and allegations of coordination. Neither the loan itself nor the alignment between Le Pen’s positions and Kremlin interests proves that her current statements were made at the direction of Russian intelligence services. Nevertheless, their potential consequences objectively align with several of Moscow’s strategic objectives: Particularly revealing is Le Pen’s refusal to identify Russia as Europe’s principal security threat. Combined with her intention to reduce assistance to Ukraine, this reflects a political approach in which Russian aggression would cease to be the defining consideration in European security policy. Thus, regardless of whether direct coordination with Moscow exists, implementing Le Pen’s proposed policies could create more favorable conditions for the Kremlin to continue its war and exert political pressure on Europe. item.title: Ukrainian strikes on Yandex’s data centers could set back Russia’s AI development by years. Never a rival to the U.S. or China in AI, Russia may now fall behind Kazakhstan, too.
item.description: Ukrainian attacks on Yandex’s data centers have hit key growth areas for Russia’s leading IT company: search and AI. All three Yandex supercomputers — Chervonenkis, Lyapunov, and Galushkin — likely suffered serious damage from fire and smoke. Soot may have reached their electronics through cooling systems that use outside air. Cleaning could take months, while replacing damaged NVIDIA chips could take years because of equipment shortages. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Chervonenkis ranked 19th on the list of the world’s top 500 supercomputers. Now Russia risks falling behind Kazakhstan in the AI race as early as November. T-invariant spoke to computing specialists about the potential consequences of the Ukrainian military’s attacks for Yandex, both as a business and as Russia’s IT leader. Meduza is publishing the article in full.
